items.stem: What is the primary benefit of closed-loop (feedback) control over open-loop control?

options.text: It corrects for disturbances and model errors using the measured output
options.rationale: Correct: feedback compares output to setpoint and acts on the error.
Closed-loop control depends on measuring the output.
Feedback can add cost; its benefit is accuracy and robustness.

options.text: It eliminates the need for an actuator
options.rationale: An actuator is still required to affect the plant.

items.explanation: Correct: feedback compares output to setpoint and acts on the error.

items.stem: Which TWO effects are typically associated with increasing the integral term in a PID controller? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It drives steady-state error toward zero
options.rationale: Correct: integral action accumulates error until it is removed.

options.text: It can reduce stability margins and increase overshoot
options.rationale: Correct: too much integral action tends to destabilise the loop.

options.text: It instantly removes all measurement noise
options.rationale: Noise handling is more about derivative filtering, not integral action.

options.text: It has no effect on steady-state error
options.rationale: Removing steady-state error is exactly what integral action does.

items.explanation: Correct: integral action accumulates error until it is removed.

items.stem: A system's transfer function has a pole in the right half of the s-plane. What does this imply?

options.rationale: Correct: a right-half-plane pole produces a growing response.
Damping classification does not make an RHP pole stable.

options.text: The system has no steady-state error
options.rationale: Pole location governs stability, not that claim.

options.text: The system is faster but stable
options.rationale: An RHP pole means instability, not merely speed.

items.explanation: Correct: a right-half-plane pole produces a growing response.
